_comment: The 注音符號 alphabet, as Taiwan teaches it. Hand-authored; no model wrote
any of this. It sits outside content/units/ on purpose: it is not
curriculum, and a unit of bare bopomofo would be refused by the scope
validator, which quite rightly insists every character be one the learner
`voice` is a Han character, not the symbol, because text-to-speech cannot
pronounce a bare ㄅ. Each one carries that symbol's conventional teaching
sound: consonants get the ㄅㄛ/ㄆㄛ/ㄇㄛ reading Taiwanese children recite,
`order` is the recitation order, which is the thing to learn: a Taiwanese
dictionary, a phone keyboard and a class register are all sorted by it.

lessons.title: ㄅㄆㄇㄈ
lessons.subtitle: The four everyone starts with
lessons.note: These four are what 注音 is named after in conversation — Taiwanese people call the whole system ㄅㄆㄇㄈ, the way English speakers say 'the ABCs'. All four are made at the lips.

lessons.title: ㄉㄊㄋㄌ
lessons.subtitle: Tongue against the teeth
lessons.note: The tongue tip touches just behind the upper teeth for all four. ㄉ and ㄊ differ only in the puff of air — hold a hand in front of your mouth and you will feel ㄊ but not ㄉ.

lessons.title: ㄍㄎㄏ
lessons.subtitle: Back of the throat
lessons.note: Made at the soft palate, right at the back. ㄏ is softer than English 'h' — closer to the sound in Scottish 'loch' than to 'hat'.

lessons.title: ㄐㄑㄒ
lessons.subtitle: The smiling three
lessons.note: Say these with your lips spread as if smiling. They only ever appear before ㄧ or ㄩ, which is why you will never see ㄐㄨ or ㄒㄚ.

lessons.title: ㄓㄔㄕㄖ
lessons.subtitle: Tongue curled back
lessons.note: Curl the tongue tip up towards the roof of the mouth. In Taiwan these are commonly softened towards ㄗㄘㄙ in casual speech — 知道 often comes out closer to zīdào — but the written form never changes.

lessons.title: ㄗㄘㄙ
lessons.subtitle: Flat tongue
lessons.note: The flat-tongue counterparts to ㄓㄔㄕ. Telling the two sets apart is the single hardest listening distinction in Mandarin, and Taiwan blurs it more than the Mainland does.

lessons.title: ㄧㄨㄩ
lessons.subtitle: The three glides
lessons.note: These sit in the middle of a syllable, between the consonant and the vowel — ㄐㄧㄚ, ㄍㄨㄚ, ㄌㄩㄝ. They can also stand alone as a whole syllable. ㄩ is the one with no English equivalent: say ㄧ and then round your lips without moving your tongue.

lessons.title: ㄚㄛㄜㄝ
lessons.subtitle: Single vowels
lessons.note: The four simple vowels. ㄜ is the one to watch: it is not 'eh' but a mid-back unrounded vowel, the sound in 喝 hē.

lessons.title: ㄞㄟㄠㄡ
lessons.subtitle: Two vowels sliding together
lessons.note: Each is one vowel gliding into another, written with a single symbol. ㄞ is 'eye', ㄟ is 'ay', ㄠ is 'ow', ㄡ is 'oh'.

lessons.title: ㄢㄣㄤㄥㄦ
lessons.subtitle: Nasal endings, and ㄦ
lessons.note: The first four end a syllable with a nasal: ㄢ/ㄤ and ㄣ/ㄥ differ only in where the nasal is made, front or back. ㄦ is the odd one out — a whole syllable by itself, and the ending that turns 一會 into 一會兒.

lessons.title: 聲調
lessons.subtitle: The four tones and the neutral
lessons.note: Tone marks go after the syllable, except the neutral tone, which Taiwan's Ministry of Education writes *before* it: ˙ㄉㄜ, not ㄉㄜ˙. The first tone is unmarked — no symbol at all.
